newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia sees inflation below six pct in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia sees inflation below six pct in 1996/97.

text.p: Indonesia expects its inflation rate to drop below six percent in the current fiscal year ending March 31, bringing it close to the five percent target of its five-year development plan, officials said on Wednesday.
They said relatively stable food prices in January had contained inflationary pressures despite the Lunar New Year and Eid al-Fitr celebrations starting at the weekend.

"I think inflation in the 1996/97 fiscal year will be below six percent. We have achieved the lowest January inflation in the past few years," Beddu Amang, head of the state logistics agency, told Reuters after a monthly cabinet meeting.
Information Minister Harmoko said on Wednesday Indonesia's consumer price index rose 1.03 percent month-on-month in January, compared with 0.55 percent in December last year.
Year-on-year inflation in January was 5.34 percent against 6.47 percent in December and 9.64 percent in January 1996.

Amang said food prices, which carry a major weighting in the calculation of the consumer price index, remained under control, helping the government to edge closer to its five-year development plan target to get inflation under five percent.
The plan runs from fiscal 1994/95 to 1998/99.
Economists were happy with the economic outlook, with inflation in check and the trade surplus remaining healthy.
Harmoko said Indonesia's trade surplus was $764.6 million last November, compared with $995.7 million in October.
"The trade balance trend is showing an overall improvement," one Singapore-based economist said.
"We think there is a genuine slowdown in import growth, in the sense that domestic demand is slowing down, which means inflation is low," he said.
"The 5.34 percent (inflation) is a pretty good figure. It's in line with our belief that the economy is slowing down and heading for a soft landing," the economist said.
Stephen Xu, treasury economist of the Standard Chartered Bank, said: "There is nothing surprising in the figures. They are basically in line with expectations."
Another economist said the inflation figure suggested that prices remained under control, which should allow for a further reduction of domestic interest rates.
"But a further cut in interest rates might endanger the credit growth target. The central bank has to know how to keep it in balance," the economist said.
The central bank discount rate for two-week money is currently 15.5 percent.
